COLLEGE NEWS
Academic honors
Students named to the Champlain College Online summeer 2025 dean’s list include Fawn Joy, of Bellows Falls; and Natasha Shepard, of Brandon.
Student mental health
The Endeavor Lab Colleges, a national consortium of 10 small liberal arts colleges, announced completion of the first phase of its initiative to enhance student mental health and well-being. Endeavor Foundation has invested more than $8.5 million to support the project via liberal arts curriculum, developing connections to place, purpose, and career readiness. Endeavor Lab Colleges in Vermont include Bennington College and Sterling College.
AROUND TOWN
Campfire safety
The U.S. Forest Service and Vermont Department of Forests, Parks and Recreation urge the public to be extremely careful with all types of outdoor fires.
Fire danger conditions and fuels are significantly elevated, with most of the state being under moderate or severe drought. Elevated wildfire conditions are expected to continue through the month of September and may persist through October. Over the next week, warm and dry conditions continue to be forecast. Warm afternoon temperatures, low relative humidity and gusty, dry winds encourage the spread of wildfire. Nine out of 10 wildfires nationwide are started by humans.
Local fire resources have responded to at least 13 wildfires since Aug. 1. In addition, firefighters have responded to dozens of abandoned campfires that were left burning after campers departed. Due to high fire danger and extended drought conditions, campers are discouraged from having campfires outside established campgrounds, including dispersed campsites and backcountry trail campsites.
Wildfire prevention tips include:
— Completely extinguish all campfires. Fires should be doused with water and stirred to mix ashes and water until the ashes are cool enough to touch with the back of your hand. This applies to ashes from charcoal grills as well.
— Never discard ashes from campfires, charcoal grills, woodstoves, or cigarettes on vegetation or organic soils.
— Refrain from smoking in areas with flammable vegetation or organic soils. Cigarette butts and ashes should never be discarded in the forest regardless of location.
— Do not drive off established forest roads or park on top of vegetation, as heat from mufflers and engines can ignite vegetation that touches them.
— When operating chainsaws, generators and power equipment ensure you have required spark arrestors and supplies (shovel, water, fire extinguisher) to deal with a possible fire.
If you encounter a wildfire in the forest, dial 9-1-1 to report the fire and be prepared to give its location and other pertinent information for first responders.
Bridge history
ADDISON — Learn about the Lake Champlain Bridge in a guided walk from 1 to 3 p.m. Sunday, Sept. 14, starting at the Chimney Point State Historic Site museum at 8149 Route 17, at the foot of the bridge on the Vermont side.
This is a Vermont Archaeology Month event offered by the Chimney Point State Historic Site in Addison, Vermont, and Crown Point State Historic Site in Crown Point, New York. Allow about two hours for this walk back and forth on the bridge.
The fee is $9 for adults, free for children younger than age 15, and includes admission to the Chimney Point and Crown Point museums. Wear a hat and bring water. Light refreshments afterward at Chimney Point.
Gage Walk & Talk
CAVENDISH — The Cavendish Historical Society hosts its annual Gage Walk & Talk beginning 2 p.m. Sunday, Sept. 14, at the CHS Museum, Route 131 in Cavendish.
A blasting accident happened Sept. 13, 1848, when railroad foreman Phineas Gage had a tamping rod pass through his head. He lived for 12 more years, thanks to Dr. John Harlow, his treating physician.
The close to 2-mile walk includes the location of the accident, Dr. Harlow’s home/surgery, and the boarding house where Gage was taken after his injury. Wear comfortable walking shoes.
This program is free and open to the public. For more information, call 802-226-7807 or email margocaulfield@icloud.com.
AROUND VT
Shelter animals
Gov. Phil Scott has officially proclaimed September as “Vermont Loves Shelter Animals Month.” Vermont achieved no-kill status in 2023 and has maintained a 90%+ save rate for shelter pets since.
The proclamation encourages Vermonters to: Adopt pets from local shelters and rescues. Foster animals temporarily to open more shelter space. Volunteer, donate, or share adoptable pets to boost their chances of finding homes.
Apple orchards
Apple season has arrived in Vermont. Orchards statewide offer pick-your-own, cider, farm markets, and more throughout the relatively short season through mid-late October.
While offerings at every orchard vary, most sell apples direct to the public through on-farm markets, which often also include doughnuts, pies and other local specialty products. Many also offer pick-your-own opportunities, their own sweet or hard cider, cafés, wagon rides, picnicking, animals, and more.
Vermont Tree Fruit Growers Association recently launched its annual Vermont Apple Photo Contest. All are invited to follow @vermontapples on Instagram and submit photographs taken at Vermont orchards using the hashtag #eatvtapples. Three winners will be selected in mid-October to win gift cards redeemable at orchards throughout Vermont.
Visit vermontapples.org for a complete list and map of Vermont orchards, farmstands, cider producer and more.
Climate grants
The Vermont Council on Rural Development announced the opening of applications for the fifth round of the Climate Catalysts Innovation Fund, a small catalytic grant program for local innovative climate projects.
Grants are awarded based on criteria that combine innovation, resilience, collaboration, replicability, as well as serving marginalized communities and those most affected by natural disasters.
Applications will close at 5 p.m. Monday, Oct. 20. To apply and for more information, visit www.vtrural.org/climate-economy/climate-catalysts-innovation-fund online, email laura@vtrural.org, or call 802-234-1646.
Municipalities grants
The Vermont agencies of Transportation, of Commerce and Community Development and of Natural Resources announced a call for applications for the Better Connections Grant Program.
For the 2026 grant cycle, $200,000 is available for Vermont cities and towns to support more connected, vibrant communities. During each funding cycle, the program provides opportunity for two municipalities outside Chittenden County0 to engage in master planning efforts that evaluate multi-modal transportation options, future land use, and water quality.
Interested parties should submit the pre-application form and attend a pre-application interview by Oct. 24. Grant applications are due Oct. 31.
Visit vtrans.vermont.gov/planning/projects-programs/better-connections for more information.
Clean water proposals
The Patrick Leahy Lake Champlain Basin Program has extended the proposals deadline for projects that improve water quality in the Lake Champlain Basin.
The intent of this funding opportunity, originally announced on Aug. 25, is to improve water quality through planning, design, or prioritization for future water quality improvement projects, or the implementation of projects that will directly result in reduction of water pollution in Lake Champlain and its tributaries.
Proposals are now due before 5 p.m. Oct. 28. Awarded clean water projects are targeted to begin work in May 2026 and must be completed by June 2029. Visit lcbp.org/grants for more information.
Farm grants
The Capital Equipment Assistance Program is accepting applications for equipment that will improve water quality on Vermont farms.
This competitive grant program, administered by the Vermont Agency of Agriculture, Food, and Markets, can fund up to 90% of the equipment cost for successful applicants. Farms, custom applicators, nonprofits and research institutions are eligible to apply.
Applicants may apply in one of the following categories: Precision Agriculture (up to $25,000); Conservation Tillage, Cover Crop Equipment, Bedded Pack Management or Feed Management (up to $50,000); Liquid Waste Management (up to $75,000 for farmers; up to $150,000 for custom applicators/nonprofits).
Applications are due by Nov. 1. Awards will be announced by February 2026, and equipment must be purchased before June 1, 2026.
